summary: The article argues that safety must be central to youth athletic training, prompted by injuries to gymnast Emily Turner and soccer player Michael Johnson in fall 2023. It describes the formation of Parents for Safer Sports (PSS), which lobbies for funding, certified athletic trainers, better equipment, and mandatory safety policies. It stresses grassroots education and community support as essential to a lasting culture of safety.
one_line: Youth sports injuries in late 2023 sparked Parents for Safer Sports to push for funding, trainers, equipment, and policies that make safety central.
key_facts: On October 5, 2023, 14-year-old gymnast Emily Turner suffered a severe spinal injury during practice, attributed to lapses in supervision and insufficient safety equipment.
On November 12, 2023, 12-year-old soccer player Michael Johnson sustained a concussion due to inadequate headgear during a game.

Dr. Sandra Williams, a pediatric sports medicine specialist, says young athletes' growing bodies are particularly susceptible to injury, which can lead to chronic health issues or permanent disability.
Parents for Safer Sports (PSS) formed in December 2023 to advocate for better funding and resources for youth athlete safety.
Julia Ramirez, founder of PSS, calls for mandatory safety assessments, certified athletic trainers at all practices and games, and comprehensive injury prevention programs.
PSS is lobbying for investment in injury prevention education, certified athletic trainers, and quality safety equipment such as helmets and mats.
PSS champions mandatory policies: standardized safety protocols aligned with national standards, regular facility audits, and mandatory rest periods during and between seasons.
Advocates argue for government grants and other resources so sports programs can afford safety equipment, staff, and training.
Roberto Gomez, Michael Johnson's soccer coach, wants kids to feel okay speaking up when hurt or when something seems unsafe, fostering a culture where 'safety comes first, always.'
Local business owner and father of two Allen Griffith says safer sports programs mean healthier, happier kids and a more vibrant community.
The article says local leagues and schools are well positioned to influence safety standards because they are the primary platforms for young athletes.
Community roles include parents volunteering for safety measures, local businesses sponsoring equipment, and healthcare professionals offering expertise to teams.
